source: Chen, Song, Zheng, Jing, Hansen, Sun (2025) Understanding Design Fixation in Generative AI
finding: Argues that GenAI shows design fixation like people do. In a small study, GPT-4o chair-design text was less varied than award-winning human designs. Four text symptoms: surface descriptions with no mechanism, repeated themes, little change across contexts, pull toward high-frequency words.
numbers: 10 novice designers made 96 AI design solutions (GPT-4o text plus Midjourney images) for office chairs; compared with 105 Red Dot award chair entries. Share of unique word items: ChatGPT 67.4% (180 unique, 86 shared) vs Red Dot 78.2% (312 unique, 86 shared). Keyword items: Red Dot 398, ChatGPT 266. Example of fixation: prompt 'cloud' gave generic sleek tech-office chairs, tied to the cloud-computing sense.
limits: Tiny sample (10). No control for prompt quality. Unique-word share is a crude diversity proxy and depends on corpus size and style. Human baseline is a different population (contest winners), not a matched arm. Venue and preprint status: arXiv v1 only.
agent_relevance: Gives a concrete fixation symptom list we can detect by code: same theme across many samples, word-frequency pull, no mechanism. Supports a code-side check of theme overlap across samples (G5, G8) rather than asking the model if it is fixated.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Understanding Design Fixation in Generative AI (image part)
finding: Midjourney chair images were less spread out than the human award chairs on shape, color, texture, and global CLIP features. Symptoms: narrow shooting angles, repeated generation patterns, weak visualization of novel descriptions.
numbers: Mean pairwise CLIP distance, Red Dot vs Midjourney: global 16.25 (SD 3.26) vs 16.05 (SD 4.38), p=0.0238; shape 0.0700 vs 0.0592, color 0.0821 vs 0.0685, texture 0.0882 vs 0.0862, all p<0.01 (Mann-Whitney U).
limits: Global effect is tiny (16.25 vs 16.05). Tiny p-values come from many pairwise distances that are not independent. Image domain, not text reasoning.
agent_relevance: Weak for a text agent, but shows the same pattern: the model collapses to one region of the output space. Embedding distance among samples is a cheap, code-computed fixation gauge.

source: Haq, Chhaya, Pandey, Bhattacharya (2025) Is your LLM trapped in a Mental Set?
finding: Adapts DeCaro's 2016 mathematical-equivalence mental-set paradigm (complex problems first vs shortcut problems first) to LLMs. Authors read the extra steps taken under chain of thought as mental-set evidence. Result is thin.
numbers: 6 complex and 6 shortcut problems per condition. Exact match, few-shot only: Llama-3.1-8B 0.16/0/0/0 (SP, SP+complex-first, CP, CP+shortcut-first); Llama-3.1-70B 0/0.16/0/0.66; GPT-4o 0.33/0.66/0.66/0.83. With few-shot plus zero-shot CoT: 8B 0.5/0.66/0.33/0.83; 70B 0.5/0.66/0.66/0.83; GPT-4o 0.66/0.66/0.83/0.83. Steps to solve: 1 under few-shot, 3 under CoT.
limits: Six items per cell, so one item equals 0.16. No significance tests. Order effect is not clean (complex-first often helped). The 'mental set' reading of extra CoT steps is the authors' inference; CoT simply writes out steps. Treat as weak evidence that models do not show the classic Einstellung order effect on this task.
agent_relevance: Warning: a naive port of a human paradigm may not show human-like set effects. Do not assume the Luchins pattern transfers; measure it. Also CoT lengthened the solution path on easy shortcut items, consistent with G11 (think briefly by default).

source: Tian, Ravichander, Qin, Le Bras, Marjieh, Peng, Choi, Griffiths, Brahman (2024) MacGyver: Are Large Language Models Creative Problem Solvers?
finding: 1,600+ everyday problems built to trigger functional fixedness (Duncker tradition) and needing unusual object use. LLMs solve far fewer than a random person, and fail by proposing physically impossible steps. They also rarely say a problem is unsolvable. Scale alone did not unlock creative problem solving.
numbers: Single-attempt success of LLMs 35% to 42%; average human 65.1% (categories A+B+C). GPT-4 error analysis on 200 infeasible solutions: wrong tool usage 42.4%, goal not achieved 17.7%, unfaithful to constraints 9.5%. Best of four human answers is near perfect; humans have higher variance than GPT-4. Humans better on household tasks, GPT-4 better on domain tasks like farming or fishing.
limits: Problem set generated by LLMs and filtered by human check; judging by MTurk. GPT-4 and Claude2 era models. Human sample is one random response per problem.
agent_relevance: The failure is not too little novelty but infeasible novelty. A fixation-breaking step must be paired with a feasibility check by running or simulating (G3, G8). Also, best-of-several human answers beat one answer: parallel independent attempts help (G11).

source: Tian et al. (2024) MacGyver, section 6.2 prompting strategies
finding: Two prompts tested zero-shot. Iterative step-wise reflection (check each step is feasible and afforded, revise until stable) cut infeasible solutions most. Divergent-convergent thinking (first list the affordances of each object, then pick and plan) raised efficient solutions most. This is the generic-parts / affordance idea of defixation, applied to an LLM.
numbers: On 180 random solvable problems with GPT-4: self-reflect lowers infeasible solutions by 9.7% vs div-conv 4.3%; div-conv raises efficient solutions by 6.5% vs self-reflect 2.2%. For Claude2 and Llama2-13b, div-conv helped; self-reflect did not.
limits: Percent changes, no confidence intervals reported in the text I read. One run per prompt. The reflection gain needs a model strong enough to simulate physical consequences. Gains are modest.
agent_relevance: Best direct template for a defixation operator: enumerate affordances of each given object (strip the name), then compose. It cost one extra pass, so can be tested at equal tokens against best-of-N (G7). Self-reflection gain depends on model strength, and a code check is safer (G2).

source: Ma, Grandi, McComb, Goucher-Lambert (2024) Exploring the Capabilities of LLMs for Generating Diverse Design Solutions
finding: GPT-4 design ideas were less diverse than crowd ideas on all four diversity metrics and all five design topics. Temperature and top-p did not give a clean monotonic rise in diversity; the default temp=1, top-p=1 was most diverse.
numbers: 4,000 LLM solutions: 5 design topics x 8 parameter combinations x 8 prompt methods. Compared to 100 crowdsourced human solutions per topic (two sets of 50). Example: temp=0, top-p=0 gave -24% DPP diversity vs the second human set on 'froth'. Metrics agree (Spearman mostly strong).
limits: GPT-4 of early 2024. Percent differences are relative to one human set of 50. Diversity is embedding-based, so it measures semantic spread, not usefulness.
agent_relevance: Raising temperature is not a reliable defixation method; do not buy diversity with sampling heat alone. Use structural diversification (different seeds, constraints) forced by code (G4).

source: Ma et al. (2024) Exploring the Capabilities of LLMs for Generating Diverse Design Solutions (prompt methods)
finding: Among eight prompt methods, the critique step gave the biggest diversity gain: one extra prompt that edits the first 50 solutions. A persona line ('design expert who is excellent at ideating far-fetched design ideas') also gave a considerable gain. The word 'unique' lowered diversity vs 'creative' or 'novel'. No method reached human diversity.
numbers: Eight techniques per topic, temp=1, top-p=1. Logistic regression on embeddings classified all LLM solutions correctly (recall of LLM class 1.00 on every topic) but human solutions only 25% to 80% (froth 80%, exercise device 25%, powder 40%, time 50%, towels 60%). So the LLM-human split is clear on some topics and absent on others.
limits: Test sets are small (20 human vs 80 LLM per topic). Wording effects (unique vs novel) are single-run and may not replicate. Persona and critique effects are shown only as heatmap percent differences.
agent_relevance: Supports a 'generate, then edit against the set already produced' pass as a cheap defixation step (it sees prior output explicitly). Also warns that near-synonym wording changes results, so operator prompts need testing, not guessing.

source: Carichon, Sharma, Girard, Rampa, Farnadi (2026) IDEAFix: Evaluation Framework for Creative Defixation Prompting in LLMs
finding: Controlled framework: design briefs x adjective attributes x 25 prompts inspired by C-K, TRIZ, SCAMPER, brainstorming, design thinking, plus control and LLM-specific prompts. Five models. Models differ in novelty, rarity and diversity. Grok and Llama-70B gave the most novel and rare outputs.
numbers: 14,350 input prompts; 3 runs per model, averaged; temps 0.7 (Qwen, Grok) or 1.0; max 8192 tokens. Table 1 (fluency/diversity/novelty): Gemini 10.43/0.464/0.463; GPT-4o 12.91/0.431/0.428; Grok-4.1 20.16/0.482/0.481; Qwen3-30B 19.87/0.403/0.509; Llama-70B 9.35/0.485/0.556. Novelty is cosine distance from the control-prompt ideas.
limits: Novelty is measured against control outputs of the same models, so it is relative. Automatic embedding metrics only; no human judges and no usefulness check. Non-iterative single-shot setting. Preprint (ICML 2026 workshop listing).
agent_relevance: Shows a metric recipe we can compute in code: novelty = distance from the set of default-prompt outputs. That is a code-side, model-free novelty gauge (G8). Fluency and diversity trade off, so report both.

source: Carichon et al. (2026) IDEAFix, brief and attribute effects
finding: Task wording changes fixation. Product briefs gave most novel and rare ideas; service briefs gave the most conventional. Surprising keywords raised novelty and rarity but lowered diversity; negatively framed keywords added to this; 'surprising negative' gave the most novel outputs. Some models refused negatively framed briefs.
numbers: All differences reported significant (tables 3 to 6 in appendix, not read). Product briefs highest novelty and rarity at lower fluency and diversity. Procedure briefs broader and more varied.
quote: introducing defixating elements, such as surprising or negatively framed keywords, partially mitigates this effect
limits: Keywords raise novelty at the cost of diversity, i.e. many ideas move to the same new corner. Embedding distance counts any unusual text as novel, including off-topic text. Refusals removed from analysis.
agent_relevance: A cheap analogue of Ward's counter-example and of generic-parts: inject a surprising or constraint-breaking attribute into the brief. Risk: novelty by embedding distance can reward nonsense, so the final selector must be a run or check (G8).

source: Carichon et al. (2026) IDEAFix, prompting strategies
finding: All method-inspired prompts beat the control on novelty, with significant t-tests. But short plain prompts that say 'think outside the box', 'wild', 'unconventional' did as well or better than long prompts that copy C-K theory or SCAMPER. Authors say gain follows how explicit the divergence instruction is, not the structure of the creativity method.
numbers: Best-alternative novelty gains in Fig. 4 range from +10% to +41% over control depending on method and metric (for example Scenario +41.36%, C-K +40.3%, TRIZ +35.6% on one top-5 metric; Design Thinking +18%). No single method maximized fluency, novelty, rarity and diversity together. 25 prompts tested (Table 8 in appendix, not read).
quote: simpler prompts emphasizing such cues tend to outperform more complex, method-based prompts
limits: Figure values read from the text dump, not from the plotted bars; exact mapping of percentages to methods is uncertain. 'Top 5' ideas selected by the same novelty metric (selection effect). Single-shot only. Prompt wording not controlled for length.
agent_relevance: Good news for the budget: the cheapest defixation prompt may be enough. Test a one-line 'avoid the obvious category' instruction before building a multi-step method (G7).

source: Carichon et al. (2026) IDEAFix, homogenization
finding: Even with defixation prompts, ideas from five models from different vendors stay in one shared semantic region (mostly digital and tech ideas). Pairwise cross-model distance is small. Prompting raises individual novelty but not collective diversity.
numbers: Cross-model pairwise distance scores about 0.21 to 0.34 (Fig. 5a). Top-100 keyword lists overlap strongly across models.
limits: Embedding distance proxy. Five models only.
agent_relevance: Supports G4: samples from one model, or models from several vendors, are not independent. Mixing models is a weak source of diversity. Diversity has to be forced from outside, for example by code-chosen seeds, constraints or retrieved cases.

source: Wang, Wang, Chen, Jiao, Lei, Tong, Hui (2026) NexusAI: Design Space Exploration through Cognitive Abstraction and Functional Decomposition
finding: Tool that breaks LLM-generated ideas into typed functional fragments, lets the user lift them to abstract levels, and recombine across dimensions. This is the generic-parts and abstraction defixation method built into a tool. In a within-subject study it beat a chat baseline on exploration depth and coverage.
numbers: N=14 within-subject. Deeper root-to-leaf exploration (mean 1.01 vs 0.47, p=0.002). Coverage 0.407 vs 0.079 (p=0.004). CoherenceToPrompt 0.274 vs 0.053 (p=0.009). Steering ease 5.57 vs 4.31 (p=0.007). NASA-TLX temporal demand 3 vs 4.43 (p=0.049). Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.
limits: N=14, many tests, no correction mentioned in text I read. Human-in-the-loop tool, so effects mix interface and method. No test of outcome quality. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Closest existing build of 'decompose into parts, abstract, recombine' on top of an LLM. For our agent the loop could be: split a candidate into functional parts by code-checkable schema, vary one part, test (O-operators). Evidence is for human users, not an autonomous agent.

source: Wadinambiarachchi, Kelly, Pareek, Zhou, Velloso (2024) The Effects of Generative AI on Design Fixation and Divergent Thinking (CHI 24)
finding: People who used Midjourney for inspiration copied more features of the example avatar than the no-support group; Google Image Search did too, a bit less. So an AI example acts as a fixation source. Qualitative: people reused words from the brief and example as prompts, and copied then tweaked the AI image.
numbers: Between-participants N=60 (three arms of 20: none, image search, GenAI). Fixation score = share of 14 salient example features appearing in sketches. Bayesian binomial model: GenAI +0.32 (SD 0.13, 89% CI .11 to .54), Bayes factor 124; Image Search +0.27 (SD 0.14, CI .05 to .48), BF 42.5; intercept -0.71. NASA-TLX equal across arms (F(2,57)=1, p=0.37).
quote: support from an AI image generator during ideation leads to higher fixation on an initial example
limits: Human participants, image task (chatbot avatar logos), not LLM text agent. 89% intervals and Bayes factors, not p values. Fluency: GenAI total effect -0.21 (CI -0.66 to 0.26, BF 3.2); image search -0.49 (BF 46.6); after adjusting for time on task the GenAI effect was near zero (+0.10). Variety and originality lower per abstract (numbers not read).
agent_relevance: The mechanism we must expect inside an agent: the first strong example or prior output is copied then tweaked. Therefore keep the first-attempt output out of the context of later diversification calls where possible (independent samples, G4), or pass only abstracted features.

source: Anderson, Shah, Kreminski (2024) Homogenization Effects of LLMs on Human Creative Ideation (C&C 24)
finding: With ChatGPT, people's ideas were more alike across people than with a non-LLM tool (Oblique Strategies cards). Within one person, ideas were not more alike. So the fixation is collective, not individual.
numbers: N=36 recruited (t df=32 analyses, so 33 usable). Group-level: mean distance from average embedding .24 (SD .07) with ChatGPT vs .28 (SD .08) with cards; t(32)=2.154, p=.038, d=.47. Individual-level: .65 vs .66, t(32)=.944, p=.352, d=.12. Fluency 8.39 vs 7.32 ideas (about +15%, p=.044, d=.32); categories 8.58 vs 6.77 (+27%, p=.001, d=.54). Sense of responsibility for ideas 48.17% vs 63.63%, t(32)=3.21, p=.003, d=.67.
limits: Small within-subject study; comparison tool is cards, not no-aid baseline. Embedding validation done by the authors. Many tests, no correction visible.
agent_relevance: Our agent is the 'person with ChatGPT' at scale: the same model many times gives collectively homogeneous ideas, even if each run looks varied. Measure diversity across independent runs, not within a run (G4).

source: Deng, Brucks, Toubia (2026) Examining and Addressing Barriers to Diversity in LLM-Generated Ideas (Study 1)
finding: Cleanest test of LLM fixation vs humans. At the group level humans are more diverse than independent GPT-4o sessions. But inside one session (10 sequential ideas, model sees its earlier ideas) LLMs and people accumulate categories at nearly identical rates and both fall far below the maximum. So within-session fixation is human-like; the group gap comes from a shared, single knowledge distribution (no 'knowledge partitioning').
numbers: 99 human Prolific participants vs 99 simulated GPT-4o participants, 10 product ideas each, categories from three dimensions. Group totals: unique categories 28 vs 22; unique combinations 206 vs 88. Bootstrapped groups of 10: categories 26.29 vs 18.45, combinations 59.66 vs 39.15, pairwise distance 2.41 vs 2.04 (all p<.001). Within person: categories 12.68 vs 12.46 (p=.45); slope 1.035 vs 1.013 (p=.51) against a ceiling of 3.0.
quote: LLMs exhibit fixation just as humans do, where early outputs constrain subsequent ideation.
limits: One model (GPT-4o), one product domain (fitness), one prompting format (serial single ideas with history). Diversity is measured with LLM-built categories, not embeddings. Preprint. Humans excluded if off-task over 10% of time (121 recruited, 99 kept).
agent_relevance: Most useful single source for design: two separate problems, (1) within-run fixation on its own earlier outputs, (2) across-run sameness. Fix (1) by changing what the model sees of its own history; fix (2) with externally forced partitions of the search space.

source: Deng, Brucks, Toubia (2026) Examining and Addressing Barriers to Diversity (Studies 2 to 4)
finding: Seeding the LLM with a human first idea did NOT raise later diversity: the model is not moved to a new region by a different starting idea. Ordinary personas (varied backgrounds) closed the human gap but raised within-session fixation. Chain-of-thought reduced fixation in the LLM (not in humans). Personas plus CoT gave the highest diversity, 26% above humans.
numbers: Study 2: 99 humans vs 99 LLMs seeded with a human first idea, then 9 more ideas: no meaningful gain. Study 3: 99 vs 99 default vs 99 ordinary personas vs 99 'creative entrepreneur' personas; ordinary personas beat entrepreneurs and reached near-human diversity. Study 4: 83 humans vs 83 humans+CoT; 83 LLM vs 83 LLM+CoT vs 83 persona vs 83 persona+CoT; combined arm surpasses humans by 26%; CoT gave humans no benefit.
limits: Personas came from a synthetic persona set. Quality, feasibility and usefulness not rated by humans. One model. Persona diversity at the ideation step conflicts with our guardrail G4 on persona voters for single-answer problems; here the task is open-ended idea generation, not voting.
agent_relevance: For OPEN mode only: partition the idea space by external cues (assigned personas/background cues) and use brief structured reasoning between ideas to reduce self-anchoring. Do NOT use personas as voters for closed-answer problems (G4). Seeding with one different start is not enough.

source: Meincke, Mollick, Terwiesch (2024) Prompting Diverse Ideas: Increasing AI Idea Variance
finding: GPT-4 idea pools are less diverse than human pools. Longer, structured prompts raise diversity. Chain-of-thought (first list 100 ideas, then make them bold and different, then write them up) gave the highest diversity and the most unique ideas of 35 prompts. Overlap between pools from different prompts is low, so mixing pools from several prompting strategies is useful.
numbers: Product idea for college students under $50. Cosine similarity of pool: humans about 0.243; GPT-4 prompts 0.255 to 0.432; 'think like Steve Jobs' 0.368 vs baseline 0.377; HBR creativity tools 0.387. 35 prompts compared; similarity >= 0.8 counted as identical idea. Human pool is aggregated over separate individuals, a high bar.
limits: One domain, GPT-4 (2023), one pool size (about 100 ideas per prompt). Diversity gains may cost idea quality (noted by secondary review; not tested in the part I read).
agent_relevance: Strong equal-compute-style evidence: pooling outputs of several differently prompted generators beats repeating one prompt. Matches 'code-forced diversity' with a dedup step at cosine 0.8 as a code check (G5).

source: Zhang, Yu, Chong, Sicilia, Tomz, Manning, Shi (2026) Verbalized Sampling: How to Mitigate Mode Collapse and Unlock LLM Diversity
finding: Mode collapse after alignment is partly due to typicality bias in human preference data. A training-free prompt that asks for several answers with stated probabilities ('5 jokes about coffee with probabilities') restores diversity without hurting safety or facts. More capable models gain more.
numbers: Creative writing: diversity 1.6 to 2.1 times direct prompting; human evaluation score +25.7%; recovers 66.8% of the base model's diversity vs 23.8% for direct prompting after DPO (diversity 20.8% after SFT, 10.8% after DPO for direct). Typicality-bias regression on 6,874 correctness-matched response pairs from HelpSteer.
limits: Gains measured by embedding diversity and a Claude judge for quality. The probabilities the model states are not calibrated. Does not address factual-answer tasks (no diversity wanted there). In the ICCC 2026 Alternative Uses test the plain VS prompt was one condition among several, not the best (see c24).
agent_relevance: Cheap one-call alternative to many separate samples: ask for k candidates in one response with the instruction to span the distribution. Needs equal-token test against k independent samples (G7); k candidates in one context may anchor on each other (c15).

source: Jiang, Chai, Choi et al. (2025) Artificial Hivemind: The Open-Ended Homogeneity of Language Models (NeurIPS 2025)
finding: Across 70+ open and closed LMs on 26K real open-ended queries (Infinity-Chat), a single model repeats itself and different models converge on similar ideas with small wording changes. So model ensembles do not give real diversity. Also, reward models and LM judges are less calibrated on items where humans disagree.
numbers: Same-prompt average pairwise embedding similarity typically above 0.8 under top-p 0.9, temperature 1.0 (even with min-p, temperature 2.0); random pairs from the global pool sit at 0.1 to 0.2. 31,250 human annotations, 25 raters per item.
limits: Embedding similarity (text-embedding-3-small) treats paraphrase as same. Reference of 0.1-0.2 is not a matched baseline, as the paper itself says. Queries are chat-style, not design tasks.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for G4 and G9: more samples or more models of the same kind do not cover the space. Diversity has to be enforced by structure, and any LLM judge will be miscalibrated exactly where ideas differ most (G8).

source: Padmakumar, Yueh-Han, Pan, Chen, He (2025) Measuring LLM Novelty As The Frontier Of Original And High-Quality Output
finding: Novelty = harmonic mean of unseen n-gram fraction and quality. Showing the model NOVEL in-context examples changed novelty very little; asking for novelty or using denial prompting (forbid concepts from earlier rounds) shifted originality up and quality down. Scaling and post-training raised novelty through quality, not originality.
numbers: OLMo/OLMo-2/Pythia; tasks TinyStories, CoPoet, MacGyver; 750 test prompts each. Novel ICL examples (5 from top 10% novelty): OLMo-7B +15.5% on CoPoet and +5.5% on MacGyver (significant, alpha .05); OLMo-2 small decrease on all tasks. Prompting methods: TinyStories +6.9% (OLMo) and +6.3% (OLMo-2); CoPoet +9.6% and +4.9%; MacGyver -18% (OLMo) and +3.7% (OLMo-2). LLM-judge validation Spearman 0.50 to 0.52 with o3-mini 5-sample average.
quote: inference-time methods, such as prompting and providing novel in-context examples, have a much smaller effect on novelty
limits: Open-data models up to 32B; not frontier chat models. Judge correlation only about 0.5 with humans. Denial prompting ran 3 rounds with GPT-4o extracting concepts, so extra cost is not zero.
agent_relevance: Two lessons: (1) example copying is real but showing a novel example is a weak lever; (2) denial prompting is the machine form of 'avoid what was used' and can be done by code if the used concepts are extracted and appended. Quality drop means a test gate is needed (G3).

source: Lu, Wang, Li, Jiang, Khashabi (2025) Benchmarking Language Model Creativity: A Case Study on Code Generation (NAACL 2025)
finding: Denial Prompting: after each correct solution, forbid the technique used and ask again, building up constraints. NeoGauge scores both correctness under constraints (convergent) and use of techniques unseen in human solutions (divergent). GPT-4 was best; other models fell to 0 within two states. Of four reasoning strategies, only MCTS raised divergent creativity, and its NeoGauge gain was minimal and 0 after t=2.
numbers: Codeforces problems (NeoCoder). Self-correction, planning and sampling operate on a single path and did not explore divergent solutions; self-correction and planning lost divergent score (divergent diff -1.2 at some states). None of the four improved both convergent and divergent creativity.
limits: Code-only; needs a historical human solution set. Possible pretraining leakage of Codeforces problems (authors note this). GPT-4 era models.
agent_relevance: The best machine analogue of Ward-style counter-example constraint. It can be fully program-driven: run, extract technique tag, add as forbidden, rerun. Correctness is checked by tests, so it satisfies G3 and G8. Also shows self-correction does not diversify.

source: Wong, Goes, Volpe, Mann (2026) How Context Injection Shapes Creativity in LLM-Generated Alternative Uses (ICCC 26)
finding: Injecting a short unrelated fact into the Alternative Uses Task prompt steers output in different directions by context type. Random context gave the highest judged creativity and novelty; object-focused and related context gave the highest value; unrelated context raised category spread. No context type won on all metrics. Runs also passed the list of earlier answers to avoid repeats (an avoid-list).
numbers: 4 open-weight LLMs x 6 objects x 6 conditions x 20 responses = 2,880. Creativity 88.145 (random context) vs 69.567 baseline; novelty 85.433 vs 69.009; value 82.296 (object-focused) and 81.472 (related) vs 71.864; flexibility 12.375 (unrelated) vs 9.417, p=0.002; MTLD lexical diversity up in all conditions, p<0.001. Unrelated value effect inconclusive (t-test p=0.077, Mann-Whitney p=0.010).
limits: Judged by an LLM (no independent human or second judge); authors say so. One task (AUT). Context snippets written by GPT-5. Short paper.
agent_relevance: A near-exact machine version of Ward's finding that unrelated/distant stimuli can break category copying. Cheap operator: add a random distant fact before generating. Needs a gate because the judge here is itself a model (G8).

source: Gjerde, Cheung, Lagnado (2025) Reasoning about Affordances: Causal and Compositional Reasoning in LLMs
finding: Tool-substitution task (Duncker/functional-fixedness style): pick the unusual object that works over objects only associated with the usual tool. GPT-4o with chain-of-thought matched humans; without CoT it fell short. Distractors hurt humans and models alike.
numbers: Experiment 1 mean accuracy: human about 85.8%; GPT-4o with CoT 85% (0.8 points lower, p=1.00); GPT-4o other settings about 12 to 14 points below humans (all p<.001); GPT-3.5 about 47 points below humans. CoT effect at temperature 1: GPT-3.5 t(33)=3.13, p=.04; GPT-4o t(33)=6.57, p<.001. Nine-option Distractor condition: Claude 3 -18.7%, other models about -10 to -11%, humans -9.1%. Earlier work cited: innovation task adults 95.7% vs GPT-4 75.9%, GPT-3.5 58.9%.
limits: Four-option multiple choice, 20 questions, new items to avoid contamination. Choosing among given objects is easier than generating the use (MacGyver). Image presentation hurt Claude 3.5 but not humans or GPT-4o.
agent_relevance: On closed multiple-choice versions of functional fixedness, brief CoT is enough for a strong model: do not add heavy defixation machinery where plain CoT already reaches human level (G7, G11). The hard part is open generation.

source: Qian et al. (2026) CreativityBench: Evaluating Agent Creative Reasoning via Affordance-Based Tool Repurposing
finding: Part-level affordance benchmark (4K entities, 150K+ affordance annotations, 14K tasks). Models often pick a plausible object but miss the right part and mechanism. Scaling saturates. Strong general reasoning does not give better creative affordance discovery. Structured affordance-level CoT improved grounding but not creativity; the authors say it may constrain divergent thinking.
numbers: 10 LLMs. Entity correctness 0.5149 average vs gold (part-level) correctness 0.1910, a relative fall of over 60%. Action feasibility 3.586 vs physical grounding 3.200 (1 to 5 scale). GPT-5.2 gold correctness 0.1819 vs Qwen3-32B 0.2588 (about 1.5x) and highest entity correctness 0.6246. Qwen scaling: 4B 0.1882, 14B 0.2483, 32B 0.2588. Interactive mode lowers scores; structured CoT gives only marginal gain. Preliminary test on 100 MacGyver tasks: CoT improves grounding, not creativity.
limits: Benchmark built from an LLM-assisted knowledge base; single gold answer per task. Scores partly LLM-judged. Preprint v2.
agent_relevance: Caution for the generic-parts method: naming parts is not enough; the model must map parts to physical attributes. A knowledge-base lookup (code) of object parts and attributes would add what the model lacks. Also, more reasoning did not help creativity here, consistent with G11.

source: Jiang, Ilievski, Ma, Sourati (2023) BRAINTEASER: Lateral Thinking Puzzles for Large Language Models (EMNLP 2023)
finding: Lateral puzzles that defeat default commonsense (a fixation proxy). Models are far below people and often pick the default-association answer or a memorized one. Commonsense knowledge injection hurt on sentence puzzles. Consistency across rewritten versions of the same puzzle is poor.
numbers: 1,119 items (627 sentence, 492 word puzzles, incl. reconstructions), multiple choice, random = 25%. ChatGPT 63% (sentence) and 53% (word) vs human 92%. ChatGPT fails 45% (RoBERTa-L 61%) of original puzzles that it answers correctly in the contextual reconstruction. Examples: 'no wings but flies' answered 'eagle'.
limits: 2023 models; later reasoning models likely score much higher. Multiple-choice format, not open generation. Few-shot with 2 to 8 demos gave limited benefit.
agent_relevance: Our own BRAINTEASER benchmark target. Shows the failure type: pull to the strongest association. Fix to test: S6 impasse operator that bans the leading association and re-asks (denial), triggered only by a failed check or disagreement (G1).

source: Chen, Zhu, Huang, Wang (2026) MedEinst: Benchmarking the Einstellung Effect in Medical LLMs
finding: Counterfactual pairs: a control case and a trap case with altered discriminating evidence that flips the diagnosis. Frontier models score well on the control but often keep the old diagnosis on the trap (Einstellung). Stronger models showed higher trap rates in places. An agent that forces evidence-by-evidence causal checks cut the trap rate.
numbers: 5,383 paired cases, 49 diseases, 17 LLMs. Bias trap rate: Gemini-2.5-pro 60.90% (accuracy 53.58), GPT-5 51.87% (54.30), Claude-Sonnet-4.5 42.98% (42.09), Qwen3-32B 43.46% (40.25), Baichuan-M2-32B 66.10%. ECR-Agent on Qwen3-32B: accuracy 69.49%, robust accuracy 24.21%, trap rate 33.75%. Ablation: causal module raised base accuracy 40.25% to 55.49%; memory module to 69.49%. Multi-agent baselines MDAgent 40.34% and DyLAN 41.69% trap rate.
limits: Medical domain; author-built benchmark; agent is a complex multi-part system, compute not matched against plain baselines. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Counterfactual-pair test is a ready design for measuring set effects in our agent: same item, one discriminating fact flipped. Also shows debate-like multi-agent setups did no better (G9). The 'check evidence, not prior' remedy fits G2/G3.

source: Kumar, Vincentius, Jordan, Anderson (2025) Human Creativity in the Age of LLMs (CHI 25)
finding: Two pre-registered experiments. LLM help gave short-term boosts, but afterwards, when people worked alone, originality and diversity of ideas did not improve and sometimes fell, a homogenization carry-over. Guidance from a coach-like LLM also left people worse on the unassisted convergent test.
numbers: 1,100 participants in total; conditions: no help, standard LLM answers, coach-like LLM guidance; three exposure rounds then an unassisted test. Divergent tasks and Remote Associates Test for convergent thinking. Exact effect sizes not read.
limits: Human outcomes after LLM exposure, not machine fixation. I read the abstract, introduction and related work only, not result tables.
agent_relevance: Supports caution about letting a model's earlier output sit in its own context: exposure to its own or others' answers sets the style of later ones. Keep generation calls independent where diversity is wanted.

source: Wen, Phung, Mehrotra, Gulwani, Beaty, Nagashima, Singla (2026) Exploration vs. Fixation: Scaffolding Divergent and Convergent Thinking for Human-AI Co-Creation (HAICo)
finding: System built on the Geneplore split: a Divergent mode that brainstorms REMOTE concepts using associative prompting, and a Convergent mode that refines a chosen idea. Chatbots that render an artifact immediately cause premature convergence and anchoring to the first output. HAICo beat ChatGPT on novelty and diversity of images.
numbers: Within-subjects N=24, poster image task; Wilcoxon signed-rank at alpha .05. Ablation reports associative-thinking prompting gives significantly higher idea diversity than non-associative prompting (values not read).
limits: Human-in-the-loop image co-creation; N=24; exact statistics in results tables not read. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Second implementation of an explicit divergent/convergent mode switch with remote-concept exploration first. Link to the Geneplore subfield. Suggests: show ideas as abstract concepts before rendering them as full attempts, to avoid anchoring on the first fully formed output.

source: Chang, Chang, Kaya (2025) Semantic Anchoring in LLMs: Thresholds, Transfer, and Geometric Correlates
finding: Theory and tests of how in-context examples bind a model's behavior: anchoring strength S = rho_d - d_r - log k (cohesion of target, mismatch from prior, anchor budget k). Two bad examples can flip '2 - 3' from -1 to 23. Predicts threshold-like flips, not smooth drift.
numbers: Three experiments (cross-domain rebinding in text and vision; numeral bases 8/9/10; layer-wise geometry). Detailed numbers not read; only abstract and introduction examined.
limits: Theory-heavy; the formula is fitted by the authors; only the opening was read. Not a creativity paper.
agent_relevance: Gives a mechanism for why examples copy into outputs: the stronger the shown cluster, the harder the flip. Hints that a few examples give threshold behavior, so test the number of shown examples as a variable (0, 1, 3).

source: Cheng and Zhang (2025) Inspiration booster or creative fixation? Dual mechanisms of LLMs in shaping individual creativity in tasks of different complexity (Humanities and Social Sciences Communications)
finding: Search-record abstract only (full text did not open, page 404). Reported: LLM partner raised creativity on simple tasks (inspiration) and lowered it on complex tasks (fixation); constraining or batching the LLM response reduced fixation on complex tasks but weakened the benefit on simple ones.
numbers: No sample sizes or effect sizes seen.
limits: Not read beyond abstract snippet; numbers unknown. Cited by IDEAFix as evidence that fixation grows with task complexity.
agent_relevance: Suggests a dial: use model examples as stimuli on easy parts but withhold them on hard parts. Verify before use.

source: Open Role-Playing with Delta-Engines (2024)
finding: Search-snippet only. Claims naive prompts such as 'use your imagination' give no useful clue to an LLM, and supplying an explicit prototype paragraph as imaginative foundation works better (T. rex prototype to design a creature).
numbers: No numbers seen.
limits: Not opened. Prompting idea, not a test of Ward's structured imagination. I found no source measuring which properties an LLM copies from known categories when asked for novel creatures (a gap).
agent_relevance: Gap note: no direct LLM replication of Ward's creature-drawing or alien-design studies was found. This is an open test for us: count how many standard-category features (bilateral symmetry, eyes, limbs) appear in LLM-described aliens, with and without a 'violate category defaults' instruction.
